note: Module blueprints for the content-production pipeline (packages/learning/src/library.ts). A blueprint holds the teaching text a person wrote; synthesis adds questions from the problem family, each checked by the family's independent check. Original, CC0, written with AI assistance, not educator-reviewed: every synthesised module starts as a draft in content/learning/review.v1.json.

blueprints.title: Work out powers
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: A power is repeated multiplication
text: 2⁵ means 2 multiplied by itself 5 times. The small raised number (the power) counts how many 2s there are; it is not a number to multiply by.

screens.title: Count them out
text: Write the number as many times as the power says, with × between them. Then multiply two at a time.

strategies.title: Build it up one step at a time

screens.title: Multiply again and again
text: Start with the number and multiply by it again for each extra power. That is one multiplication fewer than the power.

strategies.title: Use the multiplication facts you know

screens.title: Each step is a fact
text: Every step of a power is a multiplication fact: 2 × 2 = 4, 4 × 2 = 8, 8 × 2 = 16. If a step is slow, say that times table first.

blueprints.title: Expand a bracket: a(x + b)
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: The number outside multiplies everything inside
text: 3(x + 4) means three lots of (x + 4): (x + 4) + (x + 4) + (x + 4). That is three x's and three 4s.
chapter.tip: Multiply every term in the bracket, not only the first one.

screens.title: Split the rectangle
text: Draw a rectangle a high and x + b long. Split the long side into x and b. The two parts have areas a × x and a × b; together they are the whole rectangle.

screens.title: Multiply along each arrow
text: Draw an arrow from the number outside the bracket to each term inside it, and multiply along each arrow.

screens.title: The last term is a fact
text: The number at the end is the number outside times the number inside: 3 × 4 = 12. If that fact is slow, rebuild it from one you know: 3 × 4 is 3 × 2 doubled.

blueprints.title: Expand (x + a)(x + b)
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Four products
text: In (x + 2)(x + 5), each term of the first bracket multiplies each term of the second: x × x, x × 5, 2 × x and 2 × 5.
chapter.tip: The x term is the SUM of the two numbers; the last term is their PRODUCT.

screens.title: Fill the four cells
text: Draw a 2 by 2 grid. Write x and a along the top, x and b down the side. Fill each cell with the product of its row and column, then add the two cells that have an x.

screens.title: Two of the four products have an x
text: Multiply the first terms, the outer terms, the inner terms and the last terms. The outer and inner products are the two x terms: add them.

screens.title: Keep each sign
text: When a number is negative, keep its sign in each product. The x term is the sum of the two signed products, so a negative product makes it smaller.

strategies.title: (a + b)²: why the middle term is 2ab

screens.title: The idea
text: (a + b)² = (a + b)(a + b). Multiplying every term by every term gives a×a, a×b, b×a and b×b.
a×b and b×a are the same, and there are TWO of them: a² + 2ab + b². The area picture shows them as two equal rectangles.
math: The box is the x coefficient: 20

screens.title: Another example
text: The same idea on a different question.
math: The box is the x coefficient: -48

screens.title: Multiply it out
text: Write (px + q)² as (px + q)(px + q) and multiply each term by each term.
The two middle products come out equal, so the middle term is doubled.

screens.title: Another way: Multiply it out: four products
text: The same answer by another valid method.

screens.title: The middle term is 2ab: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to write the middle term as ab. The identity has 2ab: the two products 5x × 7 and 7 × 5x are both there.
There are two middle products, a×b and b×a; together they make 2ab.
math: Check at x = 1: the left side is 144. With the middle term 70: 25 + 70 + 49 = 144. With 35 instead: 109, which is not 144.

screens.title: The middle term is 2ab: solved correctly
text: Each step, then the answer.
math: The box is the x coefficient: 70

strategies.title: The sign of the middle term

screens.title: The sign of the middle term: a common mix-up
text: The middle term of (a + b)² is +2ab.
Square of a sum: +2ab. Square of a difference: −2ab.
math: Check at x = 1: the left side is 81. With the middle term 40: 25 + 40 + 16 = 81. With -40 instead: 1, which is not 81.

screens.title: The sign of the middle term: solved correctly
text: Each step, then the answer.
math: The box is the x coefficient: 40

blueprints.title: Differentiate powers of x
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: The power rule
text: To differentiate k xⁿ, bring the power down as a factor and lower the power by one: the derivative is k n xⁿ⁻¹. Then put in the value of x.
chapter.tip: Lower the power first, then substitute.

strategies.title: A derivative is a rate of change

screens.title: Not the value: how fast it changes
text: f′(3) is how fast f is changing at x = 3, not the value f(3). For f(x) = x², the values at 2.9, 3 and 3.1 are 8.41, 9 and 9.61: they rise by 1.2 over 0.2, which is 6 per unit, and the rule gives 2 × 3 = 6.

screens.title: In this order
text: Multiply the coefficient by the power, then take one off the power. Only then put in the number.

screens.title: A power is repeated multiplication
text: 2² = 2 × 2 = 4 and 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. A power is not the number times the power: 2³ is not 6.

blueprints.title: Integrate powers of x
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Reverse the power rule
text: Differentiating xⁿ⁺¹ ⁄ (n + 1) gives xⁿ. So an antiderivative of k xⁿ is k xⁿ⁺¹ ⁄ (n + 1): raise the power by one, then divide by the new power.
math: ∫ k xⁿ dx = k xⁿ⁺¹ ⁄ (n + 1) + C

chapter.title: Between two limits
text: For a definite integral, work out the antiderivative F at the upper limit and at the lower limit, then subtract: F(upper) − F(lower). The constant C cancels.

screens.title: Undo, then check
text: Whatever antiderivative you write, differentiate it: you must get back the function you started with. x³ differentiates to 3x², so ∫ 3x² dx = x³ + C.

screens.title: Two moves, then the limits
text: Add one to the power, then divide by that new power. Then put in the upper limit and the lower limit, and subtract.

screens.title: What the working needs
text: The working needs powers (2³ = 8) and fractions with the same denominator (16⁄3 − 2⁄3 = 14⁄3). If either is slow, practise it first; the integration itself is two moves.

blueprints.title: Integrate by substitution
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Spot u and du
text: In ∫ 2x(x² + 1)² dx, call the inside of the bracket u = x² + 1. Its derivative, 2x, is already there: du = 2x dx. So the integral is ∫ u² du.

chapter.title: Change the limits
text: With limits, change them too: put each x limit into u = x² + 1, and integrate between those u values. You never go back to x.
chapter.tip: Using the x limits for u is the most common slip.

screens.title: Nothing left to divide by
text: du ⁄ dx = 2x, so a small change dx in x changes u by 2x dx. The 2x in the integral is exactly what turns dx into du: there is no extra 2 to divide by.

strategies.title: Make a little table of limits

screens.title: x row, u row
text: Write two rows, x and u. Under x put the two limits; under u put x² + c for each. Then integrate in u between the u values.

screens.title: The last step is arithmetic
text: The last step is powers of whole numbers, like 2³ = 8 and 5³ = 125, then a subtraction and a division. A power is repeated multiplication, not the number times the power.

blueprints.title: How many solutions? The discriminant
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: b² − 4ac decides
text: For ax² + bx + c = 0, work out the discriminant b² − 4ac. Positive: two different real solutions. Zero: one (repeated) solution. Negative: no real solutions.
chapter.tip: b² is never negative, even when b is.

screens.title: Crossings
text: y = x² + bx + c is a U-shaped curve. Two solutions: it crosses the x-axis twice. One: it just touches it. None: it stays above it. The discriminant tells you which, without drawing.

strategies.title: Write each part with its sign

screens.title: b², then 4ac, then subtract
text: Write b², then 4ac with c's own sign, then subtract.

screens.title: Two sign facts
text: Taking away a negative number adds: 16 − (−20) = 36. And a square is never negative: (−4)² = 16.

blueprints.title: Solving a quadratic by factorising
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: If a product is zero, a factor is zero
text: x² + px + q = 0 factorises into (x − r)(x − s) = 0. A product is zero only when one of its factors is zero: x − r = 0 gives x = r, and x − s = 0 gives x = s.
chapter.tip: The sign flips: (x − 5) = 0 gives x = 5, not −5.

strategies.title: Two steps: factorise, then read off

screens.title: Factorise, then set each bracket to zero
text: Step 1: find two numbers that multiply to the constant and add to the x coefficient. Step 2: write (x + m)(x + n) = 0. Step 3: each bracket equal to 0 gives one solution.

strategies.title: The sign flips when you solve

screens.title: Why signs flip
text: The number in the bracket and the solution have opposite signs. (x − 5) = 0 means x = 5, because you add 5 to both sides. (x + 2) = 0 means x = −2, because you subtract 2 from both sides.

screens.title: Put each root back in
text: Substitute each solution into the original equation. If x² + px + q = 0 with that value of x, the solution is correct. This catches sign errors and wrong factor pairs.

blueprints.title: A limit that needs factorising
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: 0 ⁄ 0 does not mean the limit is 0
text: When substituting x = a gives 0 ⁄ 0, the expression is indeterminate, not zero. Simplify first: factorise the numerator, cancel the common factor, then substitute.
chapter.tip: Never leave a limit as 0 ⁄ 0. Factorise and cancel first.

strategies.title: Spot the difference of two squares

screens.title: x² − a² = (x − a)(x + a)
text: The numerator x² − a² factorises as (x − a)(x + a). The denominator x − a cancels with one of the factors, leaving x + a. Then put x = a to get 2a.

screens.title: The order matters
text: Substituting into 0 ⁄ 0 gives nothing useful. Cancel the factor that makes both zero. Only then substitute: the simplified expression has a well-defined value.

screens.title: Expand the brackets back
text: (x − 3)(x + 3) = x² + 3x − 3x − 9 = x² − 9. If this is not what you started with, the factorisation is wrong. A difference of two squares always has this shape.

blueprints.title: Solving a trig equation in [0, 2π)
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: One reference angle, several solutions
text: To solve sin x = k, first find the reference angle α from the standard values. Then place it in every quadrant where sin has the right sign: sin is positive in quadrants I and II, negative in III and IV.
In 0 ≤ x < 2π, sin x = k usually has two solutions (one exception: when k = 1 or −1, there is one).
math: sin x = √2/2: the reference angle is π/4
sin is positive in I and II: x = π/4 or x = π − π/4 = 3π/4
chapter.tip: The principal value from your calculator is only one solution. Always check all the quadrants.

screens.title: ASTC: which ratios are positive
text: In quadrant I, all ratios are positive. In II, only sin. In III, only tan. In IV, only cos. The mnemonic ASTC (All, Sin, Tan, Cos) gives the sign in each quadrant. Place the reference angle in every quadrant that matches.

strategies.title: Find the reference angle, then place it

screens.title: Two steps
text: Step 1: find the reference angle from the positive value of k. Step 2: place it in the right quadrants using π − α (Q II), π + α (Q III), 2π − α (Q IV). Only keep the quadrants where the ratio has the right sign.

screens.title: Convert if needed
text: The question asks for radians: π is 180°, so π/6 = 30°, π/4 = 45°, π/3 = 60°. If you work in degrees first, convert each answer at the end by dividing by 180 and writing π.

blueprints.title: The median: order first, then find the middle
blueprints.author: Claude candidate 4e655e73; Codex integration

strategies.title: The median is not the mean

screens.title: The median is not the mean: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to work out the mean instead. The median is the middle value once the numbers are in order.
The mean shares the total equally; the median is the middle value in order. They are different averages.
math: Check: the total 495 shared equally among 9 values is 55 (the mean); in order, 21, 25, 41, 47, 62, 64, 74, 80, 81, the middle value is different.

screens.title: The median is not the mean: solved correctly
text: Each step, then the answer.
math: The middle one is the 5th value: 62

screens.title: Two middle values: take halfway: a common mix-up
text: With 6 numbers there are two middle numbers (66 and 75); the median is halfway between them.
With an even number of values there are two middle values: take halfway between them.
math: Check: 6 values have no single middle; the 3rd and 4th values, 66 and 75, share the middle, so the median is halfway: 70.5.

screens.title: Two middle values: take halfway: solved correctly
text: Each step, then the answer.
math: The two middle values are the 3rd and 4th: 66 and 75; halfway: (66 + 75) ÷ 2 = 70.5

blueprints.title: Balls of different counts: each ball is equally likely
blueprints.author: Claude candidate 4e655e73; Codex integration

screens.title: Count balls, not colours: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to take each colour as equally likely; the colours have different numbers of balls, and it is the balls that are equally likely.
It is the balls that are equally likely, not the colours.
math: Check: 6 blue balls and only 2 green balls: a green ball is less likely to come out than a blue one, so the colours cannot all have the same chance.

screens.title: Count balls, not colours: solved correctly
text: Each step, then the answer.
math: All the balls: 2 red + 6 blue + 2 green = 10, each equally likely

blueprints.title: Reading a pictograph with a key
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Reading a pictograph with a key
text: In a pictograph every picture stands for the same number of things: the number in the key.
One picture does not always stand for one thing. Count the pictures, then use the key.

strategies.title: Read a row with the key

screens.title: Read a row with the key
text: Every picture in the row stands for the key's number, not for one.
Count the pictures in the row, then multiply by the key.
math: The pictograph shows the favourite fruits of the children of a school. Each ● stands for 5 children. How many children chose Guava?
The row for Guava has 4 pictures

screens.title: Turn it into a table
text: Write each label with its number of pictures.
Multiply each by the key and write the real number beside it.
math: The pictograph shows the favourite games of the children of a school. Each ● stands for 10 children. How many children chose Kho-kho?
The row for Kho-kho has 7 pictures

screens.title: Half pictures
text: A whole picture stands for the key; a half picture stands for half the key.
Count the row in halves: a whole picture is two halves and a half picture is one. Then multiply the number of halves by half the key.
math: The pictograph shows the favourite games of the children of a school. Each ● stands for 20 children, and a half ● stands for 10. How many children chose Kho-kho?
Count in half pictures for Kho-kho: 13 halves

screens.title: The total with half pictures
text: Count every row in halves: a whole picture is two halves and a half picture is one.
Add the halves of all the rows, then multiply by half the key.
math: The pictograph shows the favourite games of the children of a school. Each ● stands for 4 children, and a half ● stands for 2. How many children are there in all?
Count in half pictures for all rows: 35 halves

strategies.title: How many more, with the key

screens.title: How many more, with the key
text: "How many more" compares two amounts: it is the bigger amount minus the smaller one.
Read both rows using the key, then take the smaller number from the bigger one.
math: The pictograph shows the favourite fruits of the children of a school. Each ● stands for 10 children. How many more children chose Apple than Guava?

strategies.title: Draw a row from a table

screens.title: Draw a row from a table
text: The key says how many each picture stands for.
To draw a row, share the number into groups of the key: one picture for each group, not one for each thing.
math: The table shows the favourite games of the children of a school. A pictograph of it is drawn with each ● standing for 2 children. How many ● should be drawn for Cricket?

screens.title: The total of a pictograph
text: Add the pictures in all the rows first.
Then multiply the number of pictures by the key.
math: The pictograph shows how the children of a school come to school. Each ● stands for 2 children. How many children are there in all?

screens.title: The largest group
text: The row with the most pictures is the largest group.
Count its pictures and multiply by the key: the answer is the number of things, not the number of pictures.
math: The pictograph shows the favourite games of the children of a school. Each ● stands for 2 children. How many children are in the largest group?

blueprints.title: Reading a bar chart with a scale
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Reading a bar chart with a scale
text: On a scaled bar chart each line on the side stands for more than one. The height of a bar is read off the scale, not by counting the lines as ones.

screens.title: Skip-count up the scale
text: Find how much one line stands for from two numbers next to each other on the scale.
Put a finger at the bottom of the bar and count up the lines in steps of the scale; stop at the top of the bar.
math: The bar chart shows mangoes sold at a shop. Read the scale carefully. How many mangoes were sold on Tuesday?
The bar reaches 3 lines; each line is 2, so it shows 6

strategies.title: How many more, read against the scale

screens.title: How many more, read against the scale
text: Read both bars against the scale.
"How many more" is the bigger value minus the smaller one.
math: The bar chart shows saplings planted by each class. Read the scale carefully. How many more saplings were planted by Class 1 than by Class 2?
The bar reaches 9 lines; each line is 10, so it shows 90
The bar reaches 3 lines; each line is 10, so it shows 30

screens.title: Two bars together
text: Read both bars against the scale.
"Together" means add the two values.
math: The bar chart shows mangoes sold at a shop. Read the scale carefully. How many mangoes were sold on Tuesday and on Monday together?
The bar reaches 7 lines; each line is 5, so it shows 35
The bar reaches 8 lines; each line is 5, so it shows 40

strategies.title: Read the scale; do not assume ten

screens.title: Read the scale; do not assume ten: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to take each line as ten. Read the numbers on the scale: they tell how much each line stands for.
Do not assume ten: two numbers next to each other on the scale differ by the size of one line.

screens.title: Read the scale; do not assume ten: solved correctly
text: Each step, then the answer.
math: The bar chart shows saplings planted by each class. Read the scale carefully. How many saplings were planted by Class 3?
The bar reaches 4 lines; each line is 2, so it shows 8

strategies.title: Read the scale; do not assume 10

screens.title: Read the scale; do not assume 10: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to take each line as 10. Read the numbers on the scale: they tell how much each line stands for.
Do not assume 10: read the numbers on the scale to see what one line stands for.
math: Check: two numbers next to each other on the scale differ by the size of one line.

screens.title: Read the scale; do not assume 10: solved correctly
text: Each step, then the answer.

blueprints.title: Tens and ones: what number do the blocks show
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Tens and ones: what number do the blocks show
text: A long block is a ten and a small cube is a one. The number is the tens and the ones together.

screens.title: Bundle the loose ones
text: Each long block is a bundle of ten; each small cube is a one.
When there are ten or more loose cubes, tie ten of them into another ten first. Then count the tens in tens and count on the ones.
math: What number do the blocks in the picture show?

strategies.title: Count the tens, then the ones

screens.title: Count the tens, then the ones
text: Touch each long block in the picture and count in tens.
Then count on the small cubes one by one.
math: What number do the blocks in the picture show?

strategies.title: The value of the tens digit

screens.title: The value of the tens digit
text: In a two-digit number the first digit counts tens and the second counts ones.
The value of the tens digit is that many tens.
math: In 46, what is the value of the digit 4?
In 46, the first digit is in the tens place.

screens.title: How many tens
text: "How many tens" asks for a count of bundles of ten, not for their value.
In a two-digit number it is the first digit.
math: How many tens are there in 52?
In 52, the first digit is in the tens place.

strategies.title: The value of the ones digit

screens.title: The value of the ones digit
text: The second digit of a two-digit number counts ones.
So the ones digit is worth just that many ones.
math: In 23, what is the value of the digit 3?
In 23, the last digit is in the ones place.

screens.title: Make full tens
text: Rows of different lengths are not tens: count the objects, not the rows.
Put them into groups of ten; each full group is one ten. Count the full groups.
math: The shells in the picture lie in rows of different lengths. Imran puts them into groups of ten. How many full groups of ten can be made?

screens.title: The ones left over
text: Make as many full tens as you can.
The objects that are not in a full ten are the ones left over.
math: The shells in the picture lie in rows of different lengths. Meena puts them into groups of ten. How many shells are left over, not in a full group of ten?

screens.title: Tens and ones together
text: Make full tens and count them in tens.
Then count on the ones left over: that is how many there are in all.
math: The shells in the picture lie in rows of different lengths. Divya puts them into groups of ten. How many shells are there in all?

blueprints.title: Changing between rupees and paise
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Changing between rupees and paise
text: A bigger unit is made of a fixed number of smaller units.
One rupee is a hundred paise. In an amount written with a dot, the digits before the dot are rupees and the two digits after it are paise.

screens.title: Paise into rupees
text: A hundred paise make one rupee, so every hundred paise is a rupee.
Divide the paise by a hundred: the number of whole hundreds is the rupees, and the last two digits are the paise, written after the dot.
math: Change 3,260 paise into rupees. Write the answer in rupees, like 4.50.
60 paise are left over, written after the point

screens.title: Rupees and paise into paise
text: One rupee is a hundred paise.
Multiply the rupees by a hundred to get paise, then add the paise.
math: How many paise are there in ₹12 and 5 paise?

strategies.title: Rupees written with a dot, into paise

screens.title: Rupees written with a dot, into paise
text: The digits before the dot are rupees and the two digits after it are paise.
Multiply the rupees by a hundred to get paise, then add the paise after the dot. That is the same as reading all the digits without the dot.

blueprints.title: Changing between units of length
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Changing between units of length
text: A bigger unit is made of a fixed number of smaller units.

Ten millimetres make a centimetre, a hundred centimetres make a metre and a thousand metres make a kilometre. Going to a smaller unit gives a bigger number; going to a bigger unit gives a smaller number, as whole units and some left over, or as a decimal.

strategies.title: Centimetres as a decimal of a metre

screens.title: Centimetres as a decimal of a metre
text: A hundred centimetres make a metre, so one centimetre is one hundredth of a metre.
To write centimetres in metres, divide by a hundred: the point moves two places to the left.
math: Write 846 cm in metres, as a decimal.
The bigger unit is 100 of the smaller unit

strategies.title: Millimetres as a decimal of a centimetre

screens.title: Millimetres as a decimal of a centimetre
text: Ten millimetres make a centimetre, so one millimetre is one tenth of a centimetre.
To write millimetres in centimetres, divide by ten: the point moves one place to the left.
math: Write 862 mm in centimetres, as a decimal.
The bigger unit is 10 of the smaller unit

strategies.title: Metres as a decimal of a kilometre

screens.title: Metres as a decimal of a kilometre
text: A thousand metres make a kilometre, so one metre is one thousandth of a kilometre.
To write metres in kilometres, divide by a thousand: the point moves three places to the left.
math: Write 1,600 m in kilometres, as a decimal.
The bigger unit is 1000 of the smaller unit

strategies.title: Metres written as a decimal, into centimetres

screens.title: Metres written as a decimal, into centimetres
text: One metre is a hundred centimetres.
Multiply the metres by a hundred: the point moves two places to the right.
math: The bigger unit is 100 of the smaller unit

screens.title: Metres and centimetres into centimetres
text: Metres and centimetres are different sizes, so change the metres first: one metre is a hundred centimetres.
Multiply the metres by a hundred, then add the extra centimetres.

screens.title: Centimetres into metres and centimetres
text: Every hundred centimetres make one metre.
Take away the whole metres as hundreds of centimetres; the centimetres left are the answer.
math: 903 cm = 9 m and how many cm?

screens.title: Centimetres and millimetres into millimetres
text: One centimetre is ten millimetres.
Multiply the centimetres by ten, then add the extra millimetres.

screens.title: Millimetres into centimetres and millimetres
text: Every ten millimetres make one centimetre.
Take away the whole centimetres as tens of millimetres; the millimetres left are the answer.
math: 69 mm = 6 cm and how many mm?

screens.title: Metres into kilometres and metres
text: Every thousand metres make one kilometre.
Take away the whole kilometres as thousands of metres; the metres left are the answer.
math: 2,405 m = 2 km and how many m?

screens.title: Thousands of metres into kilometres
text: A thousand metres make one kilometre.
Divide the metres by a thousand to count the kilometres.

strategies.title: Which is longer: change to one unit first

screens.title: Which is longer: change to one unit first
text: Metres and centimetres are different sizes, so the two lengths cannot be compared digit by digit.
Change the length in metres and centimetres into centimetres (one metre is a hundred centimetres), then compare the two numbers of centimetres. If they are equal, the lengths are the same.
math: Which is longer: 7 m 76 cm or 772 cm?

screens.title: Tens of millimetres into centimetres
text: Ten millimetres make one centimetre.
Divide the millimetres by ten to count the centimetres.

blueprints.title: Using a map or plan scale
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Using a map or plan scale
text: A scale says how much real length each length on the map or plan stands for. Map lengths and real lengths are in the same proportion.

strategies.title: From the map to the real distance

screens.title: From the map to the real distance
text: The scale says how many real kilometres one centimetre on the map stands for.
Map to real: multiply the map length by the scale. The real distance is the bigger number.
math: On a map, 1 cm stands for 50 km. Two villages are 10 cm apart on the map. How far apart are they really, in km?
10 cm × 50 km for each cm = 500 km

strategies.title: From the real distance to the map

screens.title: From the real distance to the map
text: The map is smaller than the real world, so the map distance is the smaller number.
Real to map: divide the real distance by the scale.
math: On a map, 1 cm stands for 2 km. Two towns are really 26 km apart. How far apart are they on the map, in cm?
26 km ÷ 2 km for each cm = 13 cm

strategies.title: A plan scale written as a ratio

screens.title: A plan scale written as a ratio
text: A scale of one to n means every real length is n times the length on the plan, in the same unit.
Multiply the plan length by n to get real centimetres, then divide by a hundred to get metres.
math: A plan is drawn to the scale 1 : 500. A wall is 19 cm long on the plan. How long is the real wall, in metres?
Every 1 cm stands for 500 cm: 19 × 500 = 9500 cm

strategies.title: A map scale written as a ratio

screens.title: A map scale written as a ratio
text: A scale of one to n means every real length is n times the length on the map, in the same unit.
Multiply the map length by n to get real centimetres, then divide by a hundred thousand to get kilometres.
math: A map is drawn to the scale 1 : 25000. A road is 14 cm long on the map. How long is the real road, in km?
Every 1 cm stands for 25000 cm: 14 × 25000 = 350000 cm

blueprints.title: Missing numbers and related facts
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Missing numbers and related facts
text: Adding and taking away undo each other, and so do multiplying and dividing. To find a missing number, ask what was done to it, then work backwards; put your answer back in to check.

strategies.title: A number was added to the box

screens.title: A number was added to the box
text: Ask what was done to the box: a number was added to it, and the total is on the other side.
Undo the adding: take that number away from the total. Then put your answer in the box and check that the sentence is true.
math: 10 was added to the box: undo it by taking 10 away

strategies.title: The box is the number taken away

screens.title: The box is the number taken away
text: Here the box is taken away from the first number, and the number on the right is what is left.
So the box is the first number take away what is left. Check by taking your answer away from the first number.
math: The box was taken away from 20 and 6 is left, so the box is 20 − 6

strategies.title: A number was taken away from the box

screens.title: A number was taken away from the box
text: A number was taken away from the box, and the number on the right is what is left.
Undo the taking away: add that number back to what is left. Check by taking it away again.
math: 3 was taken away from the box: undo it by adding 3 back

screens.title: The box was multiplied
text: The box was multiplied by a number, and the product is on the other side.
Undo the multiplying: divide the product by that number, using the times table. Check by multiplying.
math: The box was multiplied by 7: undo it by dividing by 7

strategies.title: The subtraction fact of an addition

screens.title: The subtraction fact of an addition
text: An addition fact and its subtraction facts are one family: a total and its two parts.
A subtraction fact starts with the total and takes away one part; what is left is the other part.
math: 6,712 + 4,470 = 11,182. Which subtraction fact belongs to the same fact family?

screens.title: Check a subtraction by adding
text: Adding undoes taking away.
To check a subtraction, add the answer to the number taken away: you should get the number you started with.
math: Priya worked out 5,449 − 425 = 5,024. Which addition can Priya use to check this answer?

strategies.title: The division fact of a multiplication

screens.title: The division fact of a multiplication
text: Multiplying and dividing undo each other: a product and its two factors are one family.
A division fact starts with the product and divides it by one factor; the answer is the other factor.
math: 11 × 12 = 132. Which division fact comes from this multiplication fact?

screens.title: Dividend = divisor × quotient
text: In a division the dividend is the number being divided, the divisor divides it and the quotient is the answer.
Multiplying undoes dividing, so the dividend equals the divisor times the quotient.
math: In 110 ÷ 10 = 11, 110 is the dividend, 10 the divisor and 11 the quotient. Which sentence shows dividend = divisor × quotient for it?
Check: 10 × 11 = 110, so the sentence is true

screens.title: Not both numbers added: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to add both numbers you can see. Adding them never undoes what was done to the box.
Ask what was done to the box, then undo it: the missing number is found by taking away, not by adding the two numbers.

screens.title: Not both numbers added: solved correctly
text: Each step, then the answer.
math: 2 was added to the box: undo it by taking 2 away

screens.title: Not both numbers added: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to add both numbers you can see. Adding them never undoes what was done to the box.
Ask what was done to the box, then undo it: the missing number is found by taking away, not by adding the two numbers.

screens.title: Not both numbers added: solved correctly
text: Each step, then the answer.
math: The box was taken away from 18 and 3 is left, so the box is 18 − 3

strategies.title: Add it back, do not take it away again

screens.title: Add it back, do not take it away again: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to take the number away a second time.
The box is the number before anything was taken away, so add the number back to what is left.

screens.title: Add it back, do not take it away again: solved correctly
text: Each step, then the answer.
math: 7 was taken away from the box: undo it by adding 7 back

blueprints.title: Solving a one-step equation
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Solving a one-step equation
text: An equation is a balance: both sides have the same value. Doing the opposite operation to both sides keeps it balanced and leaves x alone; put your answer back in to check.

strategies.title: A number is added to x

screens.title: A number is added to x
text: A number is added to x.
Take that number away from both sides, so x is alone. Then put your answer back into the equation to check it.

strategies.title: A number is taken away from x

screens.title: A number is taken away from x
text: A number is taken away from x.
Add that number to both sides, so x is alone. Then put your answer back into the equation to check it.

strategies.title: x is multiplied by a number

screens.title: x is multiplied by a number
text: The number written next to x multiplies it.
Divide both sides by that number, so x is alone. Check by multiplying.

strategies.title: x is divided by a number

screens.title: x is divided by a number
text: x is divided by a number.
Multiply both sides by that number, so x is alone. Check by dividing.

strategies.title: Do the opposite, not the same again

screens.title: Do the opposite, not the same again: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to do the same operation again instead of its opposite.
To leave x alone, undo what was done to x: take away a number that was added, add back a number that was taken away, divide by a number that multiplies x, multiply by a number that divides x.

screens.title: Do the opposite, not the same again: solved correctly
text: Each step, then the answer.

strategies.title: Do the opposite, not the same again

screens.title: Do the opposite, not the same again: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to do the same operation again instead of its opposite.
To leave x alone, undo what was done to x: take away a number that was added, add back a number that was taken away, divide by a number that multiplies x, multiply by a number that divides x.

screens.title: Do the opposite, not the same again: solved correctly
text: Each step, then the answer.

strategies.title: Divide by the number next to x

screens.title: Divide by the number next to x: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to take away the number next to x.
That number multiplies x, so undo it by dividing both sides by it.

screens.title: Divide by the number next to x: solved correctly
text: Each step, then the answer.

screens.title: Multiply, do not add: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to add the number instead of multiplying by it.
x was divided by the number, so undo it by multiplying both sides by it.

screens.title: Multiply, do not add: solved correctly
text: Each step, then the answer.

blueprints.title: Finding a missing digit by undoing
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Finding a missing digit by undoing
text: A sum or difference is a true sentence. When the hidden digit is in the first number, undo the operation to find the whole first number, then read the digit.

strategies.title: A digit hidden in a number being added

screens.title: A digit hidden in a number being added
text: The two numbers being added make the total, so the number with the hidden digit is a part.
A missing part is the total take away the other part. Work that out, read the digit in the box's place, and check by doing the whole addition.
math: The first number is the total take away the other part: 713 − 255 = 458

strategies.title: A digit hidden in the first number of a subtraction

screens.title: A digit hidden in the first number of a subtraction
text: The first number of a subtraction is what you started with.
Undo the taking away: add the answer to the number taken away, read the digit in the box's place, and check by doing the subtraction.
math: The first number is the answer add the number taken away: 218 + 168 = 386

blueprints.title: The third angle of a triangle
blueprints.author: Claude candidate 4e655e73 (TP-GEO-01, TP-GEO-02); OpenPath integration (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

strategies.title: The exterior angle of a triangle

screens.title: The exterior angle of a triangle
text: At C the exterior angle and the interior angle next to it lie on a straight line, so together they make 180°.
The three interior angles also make 180°. Both pairs make 180° and share the angle at C, so the exterior angle equals the other two interior angles together.
math: One side of a triangle is extended. The two interior angles opposite the exterior angle are 39° and 112°. What is the exterior angle, in degrees?

screens.title: When the exterior angle is given
text: The exterior angle equals the two far interior angles together.
So one far angle is the exterior angle minus the other far angle. Go through the angle next to the exterior angle to check.
math: One side of a triangle is extended. The exterior angle is 135° and one of the two interior opposite angles is 108°. What is the other interior opposite angle, in degrees?
Interior angle next to the exterior angle C = 180° − 135° = 45° (straight line)

screens.title: Go through the third angle
text: Find the third interior angle with the angle sum.
The exterior angle and that angle lie on a straight line, so the exterior angle is a straight angle minus the third angle.
math: One side of a triangle is extended. The two interior angles opposite the exterior angle are 34° and 27°. What is the exterior angle, in degrees?

blueprints.title: Missing angle in a complementary or supplementary pair
blueprints.author: Claude candidate 4e655e73 (TP-GEO-01, TP-GEO-02); OpenPath integration (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

screens.title: Vertically opposite angles are equal
text: Where two straight lines cross, angles next to each other lie on a straight line, so they add to 180°.
Go round: x, then 180° − x, then 180° − (180° − x) = x again. So opposite angles are equal, and all four add to 360°.
math: Two straight lines cross each other, making four angles. One of the angles is 128°. What is the angle opposite it (vertically opposite), in degrees?
the one after = 180° − 52° = 128° (straight line): the opposite angle is 128°

screens.title: Two crossed pencils
text: Hold two straight pencils crossed like an X.
Open them wider: the top and bottom angles grow together while the two side angles shrink together. Opposite angles stay equal.
math: Two straight lines cross each other, making four angles. One of the angles is 104°. What is the angle opposite it (vertically opposite), in degrees?
the one after = 180° − 76° = 104° (straight line): the opposite angle is 104°

blueprints.title: Two dice: count the pairs

screens.title: 36 ordered pairs, all equally likely
text: With two ordinary dice there are 6 × 6 = 36 ordered pairs (first number, second number). Every cell of the table is one pair, and all 36 pairs are equally likely.
There are 11 possible totals, 2 to 12, but they are not equally likely: a total is as likely as the number of pairs that make it.
math: 6 pairs against 1: a total of 7 is 6 times as likely as a total of 2.

screens.title: Count the pairs: solved step by step
text: List the pairs that give the total, count them, and divide by the number of all pairs.
math: 6 pairs fit: the total of the two numbers is 7

strategies.title: Red die, blue die: every order counts

screens.title: Every order is its own outcome
text: Colour the first die red and the second blue: red 3 with blue 6 is a different roll from red 6 with blue 3. Both are in the table, as different cells.
So list the pairs in order: each one is an equally likely outcome out of 36.
math: The pairs with total 9, in order: (3, 6), (4, 5), (5, 4), (6, 3), 4 pairs

screens.title: Every order counts: solved step by step
text: Each step, then the answer.
math: 4 pairs fit: the total of the two numbers is 9
